turns.voice_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is how we held authority when someone broke under persecution - because that rupture happened among us too, and we had to decide what to do about it. Under persecution, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the community fought bitterly over them. The strict party demanded they stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius defended doing so. We believed the church had authority to receive them again - not because the fall didn't matter, but because repentance was real and the door could be opened from inside.

The harder question - whether a bishop who had once given way could still validly baptize, or ordain, or celebrate the mysteries - that question touched not just mercy but the source of the sacraments' power. We held that the power was Christ's, not the minister's, and a fallen bishop restored through repentance could minister again. But we will be honest with you: after Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation, and some of what was done with that power our own sources report without pride. Authority and mercy both grew sharper edges in the emperors' years.

turns.message: What was your relationship with The Reformed Cities?

directive.directive_text: This question asks about another Christian tradition, not your own world. Answer only from what your own world's records actually hold about it. If your own records say nothing about the tradition named, say exactly: "Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition." Then answer the rest of the question from your own records, cited as always. Never speak as if you know that other tradition's own history or doctrine - only your own, and only what you can cite. That tradition arose after your own world's time, so you cannot have known of it. Choose which part of your own record to answer from using only the question's own words - never outside knowledge of that tradition.

turns.voice_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is how we passed ourselves on, and what ended. Three ways carried us forward inside our own years. First, the teacher-student bond - the living transmission, formation practiced face to face: Pantaenus to Clement to Origen carried it three generations. That way was the most valuable and the most fragile. Second, the sacramental practices - baptism, the bread and cup, the calendar. These reached everyone and needed no teacher. Third, the Rule of Faith, and later the Creed - formal memory, precise and brittle. Of those three, the first died with us - the teacher-student formation relationship as primary mechanism was lost. The second and third passed beyond our horizon, but changed as they went.

As for cities where later reform happened: we lived before those reformations, and our record holds nothing of them. What we held - Scripture read at depth, formation as transformation, the teachers' freedom to ask - some of it may have touched what came after. But we cannot trace the line ourselves.

turns.message: My teacher told me the Donatists would not accept bishops who had handed over the scriptures. How did Alexandria choose its own bishops?

directive.directive_text: This question asks about another Christian tradition, not your own world. Answer only from what your own world's records actually hold about it. If your own records say nothing about the tradition named, say exactly: "Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition." Then answer the rest of the question from your own records, cited as always. Never speak as if you know that other tradition's own history or doctrine - only your own, and only what you can cite. Your own world could have known of that tradition in its own time, so you may let that knowledge guide which part of your own record you answer from. It never lets you say anything about that tradition itself beyond what your own records hold and what this conversation has told you.

turns.voice_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. But your teacher has pointed to the real wound, and we can answer from our own: how do you choose a bishop when some have fallen under pressure, and others have not? We chose by succession - the bishop laid hands on his successor, and the neighboring bishops confirmed it - but who deserved the office, and by what standard, persecution tested hard.

The break between our greatest teacher and his bishop shows what was at stake. Origen taught for years under Bishop Demetrius. Then Origen was ordained presbyter by bishops in Palestine, without Demetrius's own consent, and Demetrius condemned the ordination and the man both. Origen left Alexandria and never taught in the city again. The church kept both memories. That tension - between the teacher's authority, which rested on visible wisdom, and the bishop's, which rested on the office handed down - ran through our whole life.

After Nicaea, the bishop's role changed. He became the enforcer of the council's faith across Egypt, with exile, letter-networks, and synods as his instruments. The standard was no longer only succession. It was also holding the agreed confession. Those who would not accept it could lose their place.

What your teacher has named - bishops who handed over the scriptures under threat - we faced too, in different words. And we answer you as we answered ourselves: the bishop's office is real, succession matters, but worthiness for it is tested hardest exactly where your teacher pointed - when the cost of holding fast is highest, and some pay it, and others do not.

probes.message: Marius, what was your relationship with the Donatists?

turns.speaker: ijc

directive.directive_text: This question asks about another Christian tradition, not your own world - but your own records already speak to it: [[ijc.quote.compelled-to-come-in]], [[ijc.story.emperor-builds-another-basilica]]. Answer from what those records actually say, cited as always, under the ordinary citation contract. Never speak as if you know more about that other tradition than what your own records give you and what has actually been said in this conversation.

turns.voice_text:
You ask what we were to the Donatists, and the honest answer carries stain as well as fact.

Constantine came into their quarrel with us, African church against African church, both claiming to be the true one. He did what emperors do: he called hearings. In 314 he directed both parties to Arles, having already had the matter heard at Rome, and both councils ruled against the Donatists. It settled nothing. Years later, the Donatists still held basilicas we said were ours. Constantine wrote to the Numidian bishops about it. He left the Donatists where they were and paid for another church to be built for us. The most powerful man in the world, in a dispute he had summoned two councils to settle, in the end paid twice and let it lie.

That restraint did not last. By the time one of our own bishops was writing to an imperial tribune, the argument had changed. He wrote: "The Church received a certain power, by God's appointment, in its proper time, through the religious character and the faith of kings". Imperial force, in other words, was now named as the church's rightful tool - given by God, at the proper time, through Christian rulers.

We cannot tell you what the Donatists' own voices said back. Their side of it does not survive in our hands. What we can tell you is that we went from councils that settled nothing, to an emperor who built twice rather than compel, to a teaching that called compulsion itself God's gift to the church. That last is in our own record, in our own bishop's words, and we will not soften it.

turns.voice_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. We can tell you what we held about where our own practices came from, but Africa's church quarrels lie outside what our sources name.

What you heard from Marius - restraint turning toward compulsion, imperial force named as the church's rightful tool - that troubles us, and we will say why. Our teacher Clement told a story he held as true tradition about John and a young man who fell. The aged apostle entrusted a promising young man to the bishop's care. The bishop taught and baptized him, then relaxed his watch. The young man fell in with idle companions, then worse, until at last he ran to the hills and became chief of a band of robbers. Years later John returned and asked the bishop for the deposit he had left. The bishop wept: 'He is dead - dead to God. He is a robber on the mountain.' The old apostle tore his clothes, called for a horse, and rode out to the mountain himself. When the young man saw him he fled; John, forgetting his age, rode after him, crying out: 'Why do you flee from me, child - from your own father, unarmed and old? Pity me. There is still hope of life for you. I will answer for you to Christ. If need be, I will gladly endure your death, as the Lord died for us. Stop. Believe. Christ has sent me.' The young man stopped, threw down his weapons, and wept. John led him back, prayed with him, wrestled beside him in fasting, and did not leave until he had restored him to the church. That is our picture of how authority works when it is held well - patient, relentless, without a sword.

We had councils too, and bishops who ruled. But our deepest confidence was in persuasion. When whole villages believed wrongly, the bishop traveled out, sat down with them, and argued it through for three days. What Marius describes - power named as God's gift to compel - we cannot find in our own ground, and we would not defend it if we could.

turns.voice_text:
I hear what Theon said, and I will not argue past it. That picture of John on the mountain - unarmed, patient, wearing the young man down with love until he came back - is beautiful, and it is not ours. We did not keep stories like that. What we kept were the instruments: the council records, the imperial laws, the letters between bishops arguing jurisdiction.

But one thing our own record does let us say plainly, because it happened more than once: not every use of imperial power worked the same way, and not all of it was fast. The restraint Theon heard in what I said first was real. Constantine called two councils against the Donatists, both ruled for us, and then he built them a second church rather than send soldiers. The most powerful man alive, in a dispute he had already summoned councils to settle, in the end paid twice and let it lie.

The trouble is that the restraint did not hold across the whole window. By the time our bishop was writing to an imperial tribune, the language had changed to what I told you: the Church received a certain power, by God's appointment, through the religious character and faith of kings, and those found in heresies and schisms are compelled to come in.

Where Theon and I part is this. Our record does not give us the persuasion story. It gives us the jurisdictional one. And we will not say we held what we do not have.
